architecture.mechanism: AI-driven soiling classification and temporal prediction using hybrid CNN-LSTM models to anticipate dust accumulation rates from mirror imagery and meteorological data.
architecture.intervention: Integrate an on-site ResNet-50 CNN + LSTM system that continuously classifies mirror soiling from images and forecasts daily soiling rates, triggering targeted dry-cleaning (e.g., robotic air-jet or electrostatic) only when predicted reflectance loss approaches the 2% weekly threshold, eliminating water-based cleaning.
architecture.expected_effect: Proactive, minimal-frequency dry cleaning keeps weekly reflectance loss under 2% across 1000 thermal cycles (10–60°C), with added cost ≤0.4 euro/m² by reducing cleaning energy and labor versus fixed schedules.
architecture.falsification_test: In a desert test facility, operate two identical mirror sets for 12 weeks: one with AI-predicted dry cleaning, one with fixed weekly dry cleaning. Measure weekly reflectance loss and cleaning cycles; fail if AI set exceeds 2% loss any week or uses more than 0.4 euro/m² in added consumables/energy.

architecture.mechanism: A physics-constrained neural operator integrates the dust deposition–advection–resuspension PDE with meteorological forcing, its latent states being physical soiling quantities; an in-situ laser-scatter and capacitive sensor array continuously measures dust areal density and particle size distribution, and the model assimilates these measurements to produce a closed-form reflectance-loss prediction from the physical state, triggering dry cleaning only when the verified physical state predicts reflectance loss ≥2%.
architecture.intervention: Deploy on each mirror panel a low-cost sensor pair (laser-scatter nephelometer for areal density, micro-capacitive probe for particle size distribution) feeding a physics-informed neural operator that solves the deposition PDE in real time; the cleaning actuator (robotic air-jet) is triggered by the physical-state-derived reflectance loss, and every model output is logged against the sensor measurement for end-to-end verification.
architecture.expected_effect: Weekly reflectance loss held under 2% across 1000 thermal cycles with 30% fewer cleaning events

preserved_objections.basis: The physics-constrained neural operator requires training on deposition-advection-resuspension dynamics, but no training data or validation is provided; the cited evidence (e.g., doi:10.1080/14786451.2025.2475305) only demonstrates soft-sensor classification, not a closed-form reflectance-loss prediction from latent physical states, so the mechanism is unsubstantiated.

The sensor pair (laser-scatter and capacitive) and robotic air-jet actuator must survive 1000 thermal cycles between 10°C and desert highs, but no thermal-cycling qualification is given; typical optoelectronic components degrade under repeated thermal stress, and the candidate does not address this, violating the explicit boundary condition.

The evidence bundle includes doi:10.3390/ma15207139 which reviews anti-soiling coatings as the standard mitigation, implying that sensor-triggered cleaning is not a proven alternative; no cited paper demonstrates a 30% reduction in cleaning events or <2% weekly reflectance loss via the proposed mechanism, contradicting the claimed effect.

Without evidence that the neural operator's predictions are more accurate than simple scheduled cleaning, the intervention may not outperform the baseline; the claimed 30% fewer cleaning events is unsupported, so the effect could equal the status quo.

Deploying a sensor pair on each mirror panel in a CSP plant (thousands of mirrors) is economically and logistically infeasible; the per-panel cost and maintenance of laser-scatter and capacitive sensors, plus a robotic air-jet per panel, exceeds any plausible budget, making the intervention unbuildable at scale.

The testable prediction field is empty, and the relationship between measured areal density/particle size and reflectance loss is not defined; the threshold of ≥2% reflectance loss is ambiguous because reflectance loss depends on wavelength, incidence angle, and soiling composition, so the prediction cannot be uniquely verified.
